cells.tense: Care is being shaped right now, and the people nearby can see it.
cells.act: look after what grows with a steady hand
cells.ask: Take something you're already growing that others notice — a class you teach, a plot you keep, a repair you've shown someone — and give it the steady care you bring anyway. Water it, feed it, show up, no extra push.
cells.core:
You can grow something that's seen and stay light about it. The plot gets watered, the ones you look after know it, and you don't clutch any of it to keep it alive. You shape what's developing without forcing the pace, and the room stays easy because your hands aren't gripping.

The shape of a good week here is ordinary: do the work on the ordinary day and you don't have to check whether it's landing. Give the steady hand you already bring — water it, feed it, show up, no extra push. Care that doesn't exhaust is the point, and it leaves the growing room to keep going.
cells.sheetLine: Grow it where it's seen, without squeezing.
cells.verb: making the sacrifice visible and honored
cells.place: where what is still growing gets tended

cells.tense: The care is running ahead, forcing what hasn't grown yet into a shape fit to show.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Sit with something in your care and tell two details about it that matter now from two that don't — looking, not fixing. Stop there and let the difference stand.
cells.core:
Your care has started to run ahead of what's growing. You shape the seedlings and then shape them again, because an unshaped thing looks like a risk you haven't handled yet. The people you tend have stopped being able to say what they actually need, and some have started steering around the help. What began as tending is standing in for the growing.

Look closely and separate what matters now from what doesn't — two details each way, no fixing. Then stop there. That kind of close attention refines without force, and solitude of it connects rather than isolates. The distinction you draw will serve the thing better than more shaping will, and your hands will know when to rest.

cells.tense: What was quietly given up is still standing at a door that already closed.
cells.act: persist on your own reserves through the pressure
cells.ask: Take what you look after alone and get through one ordinary hard week with it, on your own reserves — no checking whether anyone noticed, no push. Do the smallest daily act and call it done.
cells.core:
You gave things up for what was growing — years, hours nobody counted, a job set down — and no account of it survives that holds. So your hands pull back from the tender thing. What you tend gets fed by rote: the plant watered, the form signed, nothing inside moving. The care isn't gone. It's standing behind you at a door that already shut.

Carry something on your own strength again. Take what you look after alone and get through one ordinary hard week with it, on your own reserves, without checking whether anyone noticed or pushing. Do the smallest daily act and call it done. Holding without forcing is what that week teaches, and a little of it pulls the old current back through your days.

cells.verb: making the sacrifice visible and honored
cells.place: where what is still growing gets tended

cells.tense: The care is being given now, and the account of it starts after the hands have moved.
cells.ask: When you next sit down, gather in writing the small things you already did for what you're growing and the choices you made about it. Then carry on with the care as it stands.
cells.core:
You're growing several things at once, and the story starts late: as you tell it, the meals kept themselves, the seedlings came up fine, the younger one needed nothing. What your hands did doesn't make the file. The people who benefit keep no account either, so you lose the one record that would show you your own work.

Before the next round of checking, gather what you already did for what you're growing and the choices you made about it — write them down, plainly, no audience. Then carry on without adding a new job. Tending without clutching is the old form of this; pick it up before deciding whether it counts. Put the record back in your own hand.
